reply_text:
㊥ (where the narrative and the tree disagree) Codex-10's narrative shows that for six nodes the tree's cues describe a different activity from what the machine's node actually does. The clearest is R10. The cues ("is it still going?") treat it as you checking liveness. In the machine, R10 is about who starts the click: a schedule rather than you. Your version of that is "keep it progressing every night while I'm on the flight", and kimi-3 had filed that turn under R15. For the other 17 nodes, the narrative and the tree describe roughly the same activity.

㊢ (the six misaligned nodes)

| Node | What the machine does (narrative) | What the tree's cues capture | Your words that would match the machine |
|---|---|---|---|
| R10 | starts a click on a schedule, not on your trigger | "still going", "stalled" | "every night", "while I'm asleep", "on a timer" |
| R8 | measures whether the predicted outcome happened (four post-action tokens, all `:measurement-unavailable` here) | surprise: "odd", "weird" | "did it actually change anything", "did the dial move" |
| R19 | reads checked and unchecked boxes from mission files into wants (defective here: `[x]` items read as unmet) | values: "what I want", "the point" | "what's still unchecked", "is that done or not" |
| R17 | learns which patterns worked, from use feedback | reshaping: "restructure", "new category" | "that worked, use it again", "this never helps" |
| R20 | routine health checks: 13/13 tripwires clear at preflight, findings Q1–Q10 at close | alarm: "Oh no", "I hate" | "health check", "sanity check", and also the alarm words |
| R15 | one click's outcome changing what the next click reads (refused here: no two-tick correspondence) | "fast loop / slow loop", "zoom out" | "carry this forward", "next time round" |

In each case, the cues match the node's name or catalogue gloss, not what its code computes. The tree's R20 follows Beer's algedonic channel, while the machine's R20 is closer to a routine health check. Both are reasonable readings, but they predict different words.

🖖 (a pattern the narrative shows) For five nodes, the work happened but the formal record of it didn't hold:
- **R9:** the reviewer really was independent, rejected the first commit and approved the fix, but the certificate was refused because an authorization receipt wasn't kept.
- **R16:** the code is committed, but grounding couldn't be certified.
- **GRAIN-GATE:** the cascade was admitted, but no receipt was kept.
- **R12:** no Layer-2 receipt.
- **TRACE:** `traceWritten false`.

That gap is what many of your audit turns are about ("show me", "did it really"). In the machine it sits on TRACE and on certificates, which the tree doesn't treat as a node of its own. That may be why R9 and R12 hardly fire on your turns: your checking is about whether the record exists, not about independence or calibration.

㊟ (caveats) The run was defective, as you say. For R14, CTAU-CLASS, R13 and R6, the narrative describes declared machinery that this click didn't exercise. So for those nodes, "aligned" means only that what the code says it does matches the cues, not that we watched it. R11 and R10 didn't apply to this click at all.

㊭ (next step) I'd add a third cue set, written from the machine side, for the six misaligned nodes, using wording like the last column of the table. I'd keep it separate from the agents' cues and rerun the held-out detection with and without it. Whether R10, R8, R17 and R19 start agreeing with the turn bids will show which reading of each node matches how you talk. It's a small, local change. Shall I?

previous_reply_acts.text:
(codex-10 narrating a click) That covers what the transcripts couldn't. Narrating per node from a stepped run puts English on the 19 nodes that are only code. I've read the start in `*codex-repl:codex-10*`:
- **Preflight:** 13 of 13 tripwires clear, with 18 open stop-line obligations recorded as input.
- **The click:** one click is now running with wm-author, wm-reviewer, and codex-13 as repair reviewer.
- **Codex's undertaking:** it will keep agent activity, in-process computation, nodes that don't apply, and gaps apart, and won't invent activity for nodes the run doesn't reach.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (one thing to watch) A single click only covers the nodes that click actually reaches. Codex-10 has said it will mark the others "not applicable" rather than describe them. If important nodes are skipped, such as R12 calibration or R20 tripwires when nothing trips, a second click on a different target may be needed.
